extracted.intended_audience: news editors, reporters, broadcast meteorologists, and media organizations covering weather
extracted.subtask_description: NOAA/NWS rubric defining which severe weather events and contextual factors make weather 'news' — lists official watch/warning categories, magnitude thresholds, geographic/impact/visual considerations, and triggers for front-page coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOAA Severe Weather Classification System (overall rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: NOAA's classification system functions as a rubric for when weather becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the official NOAA/NWS categories and their specified watches/warnings/emergencies as primary triggers for coverage; combine with contextual factors (magnitude, geography, impact, visuals, historical comparisons) to judge newsworthiness and placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tornado — WATCH / WARNING / EMERGENCY
rubrics_metrics.description: Tornado WATCH — Storm Prediction Center: conditions favorable; Tornado WARNING — Local NWS: tornado reported or radar-indicated; Tornado EMERGENCY — Highest threat: powerful tornado confirmed, catastrophic damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any tornado-related watch/warning is a coverage trigger. A Tornado Emergency indicates the highest level of threat and demands urgent, prominent coverage; warnings based on reports or radar should prompt local immediate reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thunderstorm — 'Severe' criteria and categorical risk levels
rubrics_metrics.description: "Severe" requires: Hail ≥ 1 inch diameter; Wind gusts ≥ 58 mph; Tornado. Categories: marginal / slight / enhanced / moderate / high.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat storms meeting the numerical thresholds as severe and prioritize coverage. Use categorical risk levels (marginal to high) to scale coverage intensity and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurricane — watches/warnings and Saffir–Simpson categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Tropical Storm Watch / Warning (39+ mph); Hurricane Watch / Warning (74+ mph); Saffir-Simpson categories 1-5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watches and warnings trigger pre-impact and impact coverage; major hurricanes (Category 3+) are highlighted as especially newsworthy and likely to require large-scale, sustained coverage and evacuation reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flooding — flash and river flood alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash Flood Watch / Warning / Emergency; River Flood Watch / Warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flash flood emergencies and river flood warnings should prompt urgent local reporting, especially where populated areas, infrastructure, or evacuations are threatened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winter Weather — watches/warnings and special advisories
rubrics_metrics.description: Winter Storm Watch / Warning; Blizzard Warning; Ice Storm Warning; Wind Chill Watch / Warning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific winter advisories to gauge severity and travel/public-safety impacts; thresholds (e.g., heavy snowfall, blizzard criteria, extreme wind chill) inform decisions about closures and emergency reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold Triggers (Magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric magnitude thresholds that elevate newsworthiness: Tornado of any strength; Hurricane Cat 3+ (major); 1+ inch hail; 58+ mph winds; Snow > 6 inches in 24h (varies); Wind chill < -20°F; Heat index > 100°F sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These magnitude thresholds are explicit triggers for heightened coverage; local variation can apply (e.g., snow threshold may vary by region), but crossing these values generally warrants prominent reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic amplifiers of news value: Population in path; Major cities affected; Power grid impact; Agricultural impact; School / business closures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even moderate-magnitude events can become major news if they threaten dense population centers, critical infrastructure, or essential services; geographic context should be used to scale coverage and outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences that drive coverage: Loss of life; Property damage; Displacement of people; Economic disruption; Infrastructure damage (bridges, power); Crop loss; Coastal erosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual or anticipated impacts (casualties, widespread damage, displacement) elevate an event's news priority and may necessitate multi-day follow-up reporting and resource mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual / Drama Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic visuals and human-interest elements: Dramatic visuals (funnel cloud, storm surge); Live cam footage; Driver POV; Damage photos; Hero rescues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compelling visuals and rescue narratives increase audience engagement and can make events more prominent in coverage; prioritize obtaining verifiable imagery and human stories while maintaining safety and ethical reporting standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anniversary / Comparison Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Worst since...", "first time...", "X years since..." — comparisons to historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing current events against historical benchmarks increases context and perceived significance; use verified historical comparisons (dates, records) to support headlines and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Weather Becomes Front-Page News
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit triggers for front-page placement: Watches/warnings active for major metro; Loss of life; Mass power outages; Coastal evacuations; Visual spectacle; Disrupted major event (game, election); Climate context (record-breaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to decide front-page or lead-broadcast placement: combine official alerts with evidence of impact, population affected, and visual/strategic importance (disruption of major events, record-setting conditions) to justify prominent placement.
